name: Real World Data Deals
blurb: Drugmakers buying AI ready clinical and molecular data.
title: Real World Data Deals
answer: Precision medicine data companies license multimodal clinical and genomic data to drugmakers for AI driven research and evidence. Tempus signed strategic collaborations with Merck and with Gilead giving enterprise access to its data platform and analytical services.

reading.body:
Drugmakers are buying access to clinical and genomic data platforms rather than building their own, and Tempus is the named seller in both deals here.

The pattern is licensing, not acquisition. Merck and Gilead each signed strategic collaborations with Tempus for enterprise access to its data platform and analytical services, one aimed at AI driven precision medicine and one at oncology research through real world evidence. The asset changing hands is multimodal clinical and genomic data plus the analysis layer on top of it.

For AI specifically, this is the input side of the stack. A model for target discovery or trial evidence is only as good as the patient level data behind it, and that data is not scrapeable. It sits inside consent agreements and de-identification terms, which is why the commercial guidance attached to these deals is to check those terms before training on the data. The constraint on this kind of AI is contractual before it is computational.

What the data does not cover is scale. There are no deal values, no patient record counts, no compute or infrastructure figures, and no indication of whether these collaborations replaced internal data programs or supplemented them. Two deals with one vendor show that the licensing model exists in pharma. They do not show how large it is.

sections.body: Check consent and de-identification terms in data licences before using the data to train models.
